content: Nail abnormalities, also referred to as nail disorders or nail signs, are distinct from skin diseases, even though nails are considered appendages of the skin. Nails exhibit unique signs and symptoms that may be indicative of underlying medical conditions. Nail conditions involving infection or inflammation require medical attention and cannot be managed in beauty parlors. Deformities or diseases of the nails are collectively termed onychosis. Changes in nails can provide diagnostic clues for various conditions. For instance, short, small nail beds with redness are associated with certain heart conditions. Acral lentiginous melanoma is a type of skin cancer that manifests under the nail. Acrocyanosis is a persistent bluish discoloration of the fingers and fingernails due to cyanosis. Atherosclerosis is a disease of the arterial blood vessels that can lead to changes in the nail beds. Beau's lines are deep horizontal grooves across the fingernails. Bowen's disease is a sunlight-induced skin condition considered an early stage of skin cancer. Brittle nails refer to nails that are fragile and prone to frequent breaking. Digital clubbing is a deformity of the fingers and fingernails often linked to heart and lung diseases. Half-and-half nails describe a nail appearance change caused by internal diseases or nutritional deficiencies. Herpes simplex is a viral disease caused by herpes simplex viruses. Ischemia refers to restricted blood supply, often due to vascular issues, leading to tissue damage or dysfunction. Koilonychia, or spoon nails, occurs when nails become flat or sunken. Leukonychia is the medical term for white discoloration on the nails. Lichen planus is an inflammatory disease affecting the skin and mouth. Mee's lines are discolored lines across the nails caused by heavy metal poisoning, such as arsenic or thallium. Melanonychia is black or brown pigmentation of the nail plate, appearing as horizontal or longitudinal bands. Muehrcke's lines are white lines across the nails associated with low levels of albumin, the most abundant blood protein. Onychia is an inflammation of the nail matrix, often accompanied by pus formation and nail shedding. Onychocryptosis, or ingrown nails, is a painful condition where the nail grows into the surrounding nail bed. Onychodystrophy refers to nail deformities, which can result from cancer chemotherapy drugs like bleomycin, hydroxyurea, or 5-fluorouracil. Onychogryposis, also known as ram's-horn nail, involves thickening and increased curvature of the nail. Onycholysis is the loosening of the nail from the nail bed, typically starting at the free edge and extending toward the lunula. Onychomadesis is the spontaneous shedding of nails, beginning at the proximal end near the finger. Onychomycosis is a fungal infection of the nails. Onychophosis is the localized or diffuse accumulation of nail proteins on the side of the nail, forming in the space between the nail folds and nail plate. Onychoptosis refers to the periodic shedding of nails. Pachyonychia is a genetic skin disorder characterized by thickened nails. Paronychia is a tender bacterial or fungal infection at the junction of the nail and skin, either at the side or base of a fingernail or toenail. Pitted nails exhibit pinpoint depressions on their surface. Platonynchia is characterized by abnormally flat and broad nails. Psoriatic nails are a common nail condition in individuals with psoriasis, a scaly skin rash. Scleroderma is a rare, chronic disease involving excessive deposits of structural proteins in the skin or other organs. Skin cancer is an invasive and spreading malignancy of the skin with various causes. Splinter hemorrhages are tiny vertical lines under the nails. Subungual hematoma is a collection of blood beneath a toenail or fingernail, often resulting from trauma such as slamming a finger in a door. Terry's nails are characterized by a white, ground glass appearance of the nails, with no visible lunula. Trauma refers to physical injury. Tuberous sclerosis is a rare genetic disease causing benign tumors in the brain and other vital organs, including the kidneys, heart, eyes, lungs, and skin. Warts are small, rough tumors, typically on the hands and feet, resembling cauliflower or solid blisters. Yellow nail syndrome is marked by yellow nails that lack a cuticle, grow slowly, and are loose or detached (onycholysis).
